en: Dīgha Nikāya 18:
Janavasabha Sutta 1.
The Prophecy Concerning the Nātikiyas and Others
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was staying at Nādika in the Brick House.

Now at that time, the Blessed One was giving accounts of the rebirths of his attendant monks who had passed away and died in various regions—in Kāsī and Kosala, among the Vajjis and Mallas, among the Cetis and Vaṃsas, and among the Kurus, Pañcālas, and the Madhyas and Surasenas:
“Such-and-such a person has been reborn there; such-and-such a person has been reborn there.

More than fifty of the Nātiki attendants who have passed away and died, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, have been spontaneously reborn there and will attain final nibbāna from that world, not subject to returning.

More than ninety of the Nātiki attendants who have passed away and died, through the total destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, have become once-returners; having returned to this world only once more, they will make an end of suffering.”

“More than five hundred Nātikiya attendants have passed away and died; through the total destruction of the three fetters, they have become stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and headed for full enlightenment.
The Nātikiya attendants heard:

“It is said that the Blessed One, in various regions throughout the countryside—among the Kāsīs and Kosalans, the Vajjis and Mallas, the Cetis and Vaṁsas, the Kurus and Pañcālas, and the Majjhas and Sūrasenas—declares the rebirths of those attendants who have passed away and died.”
‘So-and-so has been reborn there; so-and-so has been reborn there.

More than fifty of the Nātiki attendants who have passed away and died, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, have been spontaneously reborn there and will attain final nibbāna from that world, never to return.

More than ninety of the Nātiki attendants who have passed away and died, through the destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, have become once-returners who, having come back to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering.’

“More than five hundred Nātika attendants have passed away and died; through the total destruction of the three fetters, they have become stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment.
And having heard the Blessed One’s answer to their questions, the Nātika attendants were uplifted, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness.
The Venerable Ānanda heard this.

“It seems that the Blessed One, throughout various regions, declares the rebirths of his attendant monks who have passed away and died: among the Kāsīs and Kosalans, the Vajjis and Mallas, the Cetis and Vaṃsas, the Kurus and Pañcālas, and the Majjhas and Sūrasenas:
‘So-and-so has been reborn there; so-and-so has been reborn there.

More than fifty attendant monks from Nātikā who have passed away and died, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, have become spontaneously born [in the Pure Abodes], attaining final nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world.’”

“More than ninety of the Nātika attendants have passed away and died; through the complete destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, they are once-returners who, having come back to this world only one more time, will make an end of suffering.

More than five hundred of the Nātika attendants have passed away and died; through the complete destruction of the three fetters, they are stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment.”
And because of that, the attendants from Nādika were uplifted, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness upon hearing the Blessed One’s answer to their questions.
2. Ānanda’s Discourse:
Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
“But indeed, these Magadhan attendants who were numerous and long-standing, they too have passed away and died.
It seems that Aṅga and Magadha are empty of those Magadhan attendants who have passed away and died.
Yet they too had confidence in the Buddha, confidence in the Dhamma, confidence in the Saṅgha, and were perfect in their virtuous conduct.”
Those who have passed away and died were not declared [their destination] by the Blessed One;
it would be good if he were to declare this as well, so that many people might gain confidence and thereby go to a happy destination.
Furthermore, there was King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, a righteous king of Dharma, who was beneficial to brahmins and householders, as well as to the townspeople and the people of the countryside.
Furthermore, people dwell praising him, saying:
"Thus that righteous Dhamma-king passed away after bringing us happiness; thus we dwelt in comfort within the realm of that righteous Dhamma-king.
Moreover, he was one who had confidence in the Buddha, confidence in the Dhamma, confidence in the Saṅgha, and was one who fulfilled the moral precepts.
People even said this:
“King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha passed away while still intent on praising the Blessed One.
Although he has passed away and died, he was not declared [as having attained final liberation] by the Blessed One.
"It would be good for him to give an explanation, so that many people might gain confidence and thereby go to a happy destination.
Now, the Blessed One’s awakening occurred among the Magadhans.
Since the Blessed One’s awakening occurred among the Magadhans, why would he not explain the rebirths of those Magadhan attendants who have passed away and died?"
"If the Blessed One were not to declare the rebirths of the deceased Magadhan attendants who have passed away, the Magadhan attendants would be dejected;
and since the Magadhan attendants would be dejected, why would the Blessed One not declare them?
Having reflected alone in private on this matter concerning the Magadhan attendants, the Venerable Ānanda, at the time of dawn during the night...
Having risen, he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"I have heard this, Bhante:

“It seems that the Blessed One, in various regions throughout the countryside, declares the rebirths of his attendant monks who have passed away and died: among the Kāsīs and Kosalans, the Vajjis and Mallas, the Cetis and Vaṃsas, the Kurus and Pañcālas, and the Majjhas and Sūrasenas:
‘So-and-so has been reborn there; so-and-so has been reborn there.

More than fifty attendant monks from Nātika who have passed away and died have, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, become spontaneously born beings who will attain final nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world.”

"More than ninety of the Nātika attendants have passed away and died; through the total destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, they are once-returners who, having come back to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering.

More than five hundred of the Nātika attendants have passed away and died; through the total destruction of the three fetters, they are stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and headed for full enlightenment."
And because of that, the Nātika attendants were uplifted, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness upon hearing the Blessed One’s answer to their questions.
But these Magadhan attendants, Bhante, who were numerous and long-standing, have also passed away and died;
it seems that Aṅga and Magadha are empty of those Magadhan attendants who have passed away and died.”

Furthermore, Bhante, there were those who had confidence in the Buddha, confidence in the Dhamma, and confidence in the Saṅgha, and who were perfect in their virtuous conduct; yet when they passed away and died, they were not declared [the destination] by the Blessed One.
It would be good if he were to declare this as well, so that many people might gain confidence and thereby go to a happy destination.

Moreover, Bhante, there was King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, a righteous king who ruled by Dhamma, who was a benefactor to brahmins and householders, as well as to the townspeople and the rural folk.
And people dwell praising him in this way:
“Thus that righteous Dhamma-king passed away after having made us happy;
thus we dwelt in comfort within the realm of that righteous Dhamma-king.”
Moreover, Bhante, he was one who had faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dhamma, faith in the Saṅgha, and was perfect in his virtuous conduct.
Indeed, people even said this:
“King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha has passed away while still intent on praising the Blessed One, even unto the time of his death.”
Thus, his passing away and death have not been declared by the Blessed One;
it would be well if he were to explain this, for many people would gain confidence and thereby go to a happy destination.
Moreover, Bhante, the Blessed One’s enlightenment occurred among the Magadhans.
"But where, venerable sir, the Blessed One’s awakening occurred among the Magadhans, how could the Blessed One not declare the rebirths of those Magadhan attendants who have passed away and died?
If the Blessed One, venerable sir, were not to declare the rebirths of those Magadhan attendants who have passed away and died, the Magadhan attendants would be dejected;
and since the Magadhan attendants would be dejected, why would the Blessed One not declare it?"

Having delivered this discourse to the Magadhan attendants in the presence of the Blessed One, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Not long after the Venerable Ānanda had left, the Blessed One dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and robe, and entered Nādikā for alms.
Having walked for alms in Nādikā, after his meal, on his return from the almsround, he washed his feet and entered the Brick House.
Having entered, he focused his attention on the Magadhan attendants, treating them with earnestness, attending to them with his whole mind, and sat down on the prepared seat, thinking:
"I shall know their destination and their future state; what is the destination of these gentlemen, and what is their future state?"
The Blessed One saw the Magadhan attendants and thought:
"Wherever these gentlemen go, whatever their future destination may be.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion, came out of the Brick House, and sat down on a seat prepared in the shade behind the monastery.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“The Blessed One’s appearance is serene, Bhante; the Blessed One’s facial complexion seems radiant due to the clarity of his faculties.
Surely, Bhante, the Blessed One has dwelt today in a peaceful dwelling.”
“Ānanda, as soon as you had finished speaking to me face-to-face concerning the Māgadhaka attendants and rose from your seat to depart,
I, having walked for alms in Nātika and returned from my almsround after the meal,
washed my feet, entered the Brick House, and applied my mind with earnest resolve concerning the Māgadhaka attendants.”
Having brought them to mind and having focused upon them with my whole heart, I sat down on the prepared seat, thinking:
"I shall know their destination and their future state; what is the destination of these gentlemen, and what is their future state?
And I saw, Ānanda, regarding those attendants from Magadha: "What is the destination of these gentlemen, and what is their future state?"
3. The Yakkha Janavasabha:
Then, Ānanda, a vanished yakkha raised his voice, saying:
"I am Janavasabha, Blessed One."
“I am Janavasabha, O Sugata.
“Do you recall, Ānanda, having heard such a name as ‘Janavasabha’ before this?
“I do not recall, Bhante, having heard such a name as ‘Janavasabha’ before this; nevertheless, Bhante, my hair stood on end upon hearing the name ‘Janavasabha.’”
"Then, Bhante, it occurred to me:
'Surely that yakkha cannot be insignificant, since such a name as "Janavasabha" has been so well-bestowed upon him.
"Immediately after the manifestation of the sound, Ānanda, a yakkha of magnificent appearance appeared before me."
A second time he announced his name:
“I am Bimbisāra, Blessed One;
I am Bimbisāra, Sugata.”
"Venerable sir, this is the seventh time that I have been reborn into the company of the Great King Vessavaṇa; having passed away from there, I am now able to become a king among humans.
Seven times from here, seven times from there—fourteen existences in total."
“I recognize my dwelling where I lived in the past.
For a long time indeed, Bhante, I have been one who does not fall away, and I perceive myself as one who does not fall away; moreover, my hope is established for the state of a once-returner.”
“It is wonderful, venerable Janavasabha the yakkha; it is marvelous, venerable Janavasabha the yakkha!

You say, ‘For a long time, Bhante, I have recognized myself as one who has not fallen into the lower realms,’ yet you also say, ‘And my aspiration remains fixed upon the state of a once-returner. From what source, then, does the venerable Janavasabha derive this?”
“Does a *yakkha* perceive such a sublime attainment of distinction?
“Not otherwise, Blessed One, not otherwise, Sugata, than through your teaching.

From the moment, Bhante, that I became single-mindedly devoted to the Blessed One, from that time on, Bhante, I have long perceived non-falling into the lower realms, and I have established hope for the state of a once-returner.”
"Here, venerable sir, having been sent by the Great King Vessavaṇa on some business to the presence of the Great King Virūḷhaka,
I saw the Blessed One on the way, having entered the Brick House,
sitting with his bones as his object, attending to them, and applying his whole mind to them, concerning the Magadhan attendants."
“I shall know their destination and their future state—where those venerable ones go and what their future state will be.
But it is not surprising, Bhante, that when the Great King Vessavaṇa spoke thus in that assembly, I heard it directly and received it directly:
“Where those venerable ones go and what their future state will be.”
Then, Bhante, it occurred to me:
"I shall see the Blessed One, and I shall report this matter to the Blessed One.
These, Bhante, were the two reasons for my approaching the Blessed One for an audience.
4. The Assembly Hall of the Gods.

"Venerable sir, in former days, even earlier than that, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, when the rains-retreat had begun and the night of the full moon was at its height, all the Tāvatiṃsa gods would sit together and assemble in the Sudhamma assembly hall."
A great divine assembly was seated all around, and the four Great Kings were seated in the four directions.
In the eastern direction, the Great King Dhatarattha sat facing west, with the gods in front of him;
in the southern direction, the Great King Virulhaka sat facing north, with the gods in front of him.
In the western direction, the Great King Virūpakkha sat facing the east, with the gods in attendance before him;
in the northern direction, the Great King Vessavaṇa sat facing the south, with the gods in attendance before him.
When, venerable sir, all the Tāvatiṃsa gods have gathered together and are seated in the Sudhamma assembly hall...
A great divine assembly had gathered and was seated on all sides, and the Four Great Kings were seated in the four directions. This was their seat;
only afterwards did our own seats come to be.
“Venerable sir, those gods who have recently been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa host after practicing the holy life under the Blessed One outshine the other gods in both beauty and glory.
Because of this, venerable sir, the Tāvatiṃsa gods are uplifted, joyful, and filled with rapture and happiness, thinking:
‘Indeed, the divine hosts are being replenished; the asura hosts are declining.’”
Then, venerable sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, perceiving the confidence of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, rejoiced with these verses:
“Truly, the devas of the Tāvatiṃsa realm rejoice together with their leader!
Paying homage to the Tathāgata and to the sublime nature of the Dhamma,
they behold the newly arisen devas.
To those who possess beauty and renown,
who have practiced the holy life under the Sugata and have now come here.
They outshine others in beauty, fame, and long life—
these disciples of the one of vast wisdom.
Having attained distinction here,
the Tāvatiṃsa gods together with their lord rejoice upon seeing this.
"Reverencing the Tathāgata and the excellence of the Dhamma. Thus,
venerable sir, the gods of the Thirty-three became even more uplifted, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness.
“The divine hosts, indeed, are filling out, while the asura hosts are diminishing.

Then, venerable sir, having reflected upon that matter and deliberated upon that matter for which the gods of the Thirty-three had assembled and gathered in the Sudhamma assembly hall, those four spoke these words.
The four Great Kings are present for that purpose. Those four Great Kings, having received instructions regarding that matter, remain in their respective seats, neither departing nor wavering.
Having been addressed with these words, the kings—
Having received the instruction,
their minds serene and peaceful,
they stood together at their seats.
Then, venerable sir, a sublime light arose from the northern direction, and a radiance appeared that surpassed even the power of the gods.
Then, venerable sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
"As these signs are seen, dear sirs, a sublime light arises and a radiance appears."
"Brahmā will appear. For this is the precursor to the appearance of Brahmā, namely, that light arises and radiance becomes manifest.
Thus were the signs seen.
"Brahmā will become manifest;
for this is the sign of Brahmā:
a vast and great radiance."
5. The Discourse on Sanaṅkumāra.
Then, venerable sir, the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven sat down each in their own seats, thinking:
"We shall recognize this radiance; we shall go only after having experienced whatever its result will be."
The four Great Kings also sat down in their respective seats, thinking:
"We shall know what this radiance portends; we shall go only after having witnessed its result.
Having heard this, the gods of the Thirty-three became one-pointed in mind.
“We shall know this radiance; we shall understand what its result will be, and having realized it ourselves, we shall depart.
Venerable sir, when Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra appears to the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he appears having manifested a gross physical form.
For that natural appearance of Brahmā cannot be seen within the range of vision of the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Venerable sir, when Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra appears before the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he outshines the other gods both in beauty and in glory.
Just as, venerable sir, a golden form outshines a human form, even so, venerable sir,
when Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra appears before the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he outshines the other gods both in beauty and in glory.
Venerable sir, when Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra appears before the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, no god in that assembly bows down to him, rises up for him, or invites him to a seat.
Instead, they all sit silently in the cross-legged posture with palms joined, thinking:
"Whichever god now desires a seat for Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, upon his seat shall he sit."
"Venerable sir, whichever deity Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra sits upon his couch, that deity receives a sublime attainment of inspiration; that deity receives a sublime attainment of joy.
Just as, venerable sir, a consecrated kṣatriya king who has been recently anointed to the kingship receives a sublime attainment of inspiration and receives a sublime attainment of joy;"
"In the same way, Bhante, whichever deity Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra sits upon his couch gains a sublime attainment of rapture; that deity gains a sublime attainment of joy.
Then, Bhante, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, having manifested a gross physical form and appearing in the guise of a youth, made his appearance before the Tāvatiṃsa devas as Pañcasikha.
He rose up into the air and sat cross-legged in the sky, in mid-air."

"Just as, venerable sir, a strong man might sit cross-legged on a well-spread couch or on a level patch of ground, even so, venerable sir, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, having risen into the air and sat cross-legged in the sky, perceiving the serene confidence of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, expressed his approval with these verses:
‘The devas truly rejoice, O friends! ...’"
The Thirty-three gods, together with Indra,
paid homage to the Tathāgata and to the sublime nature of the Dhamma.
Beholding the new god,
endowed with beauty and renown,
[they practiced] the holy life under the Sugata.
Having practiced [the holy life] and come here,
they outshine others in beauty, fame, and longevity.
The disciples of the one of vast wisdom have attained distinction here;
seeing this, they rejoice.
The Thirty-three gods, together with Indra,
pay homage to the Tathāgata and to the sublime nature of the Dhamma.
"Venerable sir, this was the meaning spoken by Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra.
Venerable sir, when Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra spoke, his voice possessed eight qualities: it was distinct, intelligible, melodious, worth hearing, clear, far-reaching, deep, and resonant.
And, venerable sir, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra made himself understood by his voice according to the assembly; yet his sound did not issue beyond that assembly."
“Venerable sir, one who possesses such a voice endowed with eight factors is called ‘one with the voice of Brahmā.
Then, venerable sir, the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, having manifested thirty-three bodies and sitting cross-legged on individual couches among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa gods:

‘What do you think, worthy Tāvatiṃsa gods? To what extent has that Blessed One practiced for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans?’”
For whoever, sir, has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, and is perfect in their virtuous conduct,
at the breaking up of the body, after death, some of them are reborn in the company of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas,
and some are reborn in the company of the Nimmānarati devas.
Some are reborn into the company of the Tusita devas; some are reborn into the company of the Yāma devas;
some are reborn into the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas; and some are reborn into the company of the Cātumahārājika devas.
“Those who fulfill every lowest body fulfill the Gandhabba-body.
This was the meaning, venerable sir, that Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra spoke;
and as Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra spoke this meaning, it was only the sound that the deities perceived.
“Whoever this is that speaks alone upon my couch,” so it was said.
When one speaks, all the emanations speak.
When one person remains silent, they all become silent;
then the gods think:
"The Thirty-three [gods] together with their Indra;
yet this one here upon my couch speaks all alone."

Then, venerable sir, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra concentrated himself into a single form; having concentrated himself into a single form, he sat cross-legged upon the cross-legged seat of Sakka, lord of the devas, and addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
"6. Cultivated Bases of Psychic Power:
'What do you think, worthy Tāvatiṃsa devas? To what extent have these things been well-expounded by that Blessed One, the Knower...'"

By the One who has seen, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, four bases of psychic power have been proclaimed for the sake of the abundance of psychic power, the variety of psychic power, and the transformation of psychic power.
What are the four?
Here, friend, a bhikkhu develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving.
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through energy and volitional formations of striving.
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through mind and volitional formations of striving.
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through investigation and volitional formations of striving.

"Indeed, sir, these four bases of psychic power were proclaimed by that Blessed One—who knows and sees, who is the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—for the sake of the abundance of psychic power, the variety of psychic power, and the mastery of psychic power.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past experienced various kinds of psychic power, all of them did so through having developed and cultivated these very four bases of psychic power."

"Indeed, sirs, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience various kinds of psychic power, all of them will do so because they have developed and cultivated these very four bases of psychic power.
Indeed, sirs, whatever ascetics or brahmins at present experience various kinds of psychic power, all of them do so because they have developed and cultivated these very four bases of psychic power.
Do you, venerable devas of the Thirty-three, see such a manifestation of psychic power in me as well?"
“Yes, Great Brahmā.
“It is because I have developed and cultivated these very same four bases for psychic power, sir,
that I am so powerful and so majestic,” said Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra regarding this matter, venerable sir.
Having spoken thus, venerable sir, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra addressed the Tāvatiṃsa gods:

"What do you think, worthy Tāvatiṃsa gods? To what extent has this threefold attainment of opportunity for the attainment of happiness been discovered by that Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One?"
Which three?
Here, sir, a certain person dwells associated with sensual pleasures, associated with unwholesome states.
At a later time, he hears the noble Dhamma, attends to it properly, and practices in accordance with the Dhamma.
Thus, by resorting to hearing the noble Dhamma, proper attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma, he dwells unattached—to sensual pleasures and unwholesome states.
In him who is unattached, who is unattached to sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, happiness arises; from happiness, gladness arises further.
Just as, sir, joy would arise in one who is delighted;
In the same way, sir, for one who is unattached to sensual pleasures and unattached to unwholesome states, happiness arises; from happiness, joy arises.
This, sir, is the first attainment of an opportunity discovered by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—for the attainment of happiness.

Furthermore, sir, there is the case where for someone here the gross bodily formations have not subsided, the gross verbal formations have not subsided, and the gross mental formations have not subsided.
Then, at a later time, he hears the noble Dhamma, attends to it wisely, and practices in accordance with the Dhamma.
By virtue of hearing the noble Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma,
his gross bodily formations subside, his gross verbal formations subside, and his gross mental formations subside.

With the subsiding of gross bodily formations, with the subsiding of gross verbal formations, and with the subsiding of gross mental formations, pleasure arises, and more than pleasure, gladness arises.
Just as, sir, joy might arise in one who is delighted; such is the case.

In the same way, sir, with the subsiding of gross bodily formations, the subsiding of gross verbal formations, and the subsiding of gross mental formations, pleasure arises; and beyond pleasure, gladness arises.
This, sir, is the second attainment of an opportunity discovered by that Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—for the attainment of happiness.
Furthermore, sir, here someone does not understand as it really is: "This is wholesome," nor does he understand as it really is: "This is unwholesome. He does not understand as it really is:
"This is blameworthy, this is blameless; this is to be cultivated, this is not to be cultivated; this is inferior, this is superior; this is dark, this is bright, with their counterparts.
At a later time, he hears the noble Dhamma, applies his mind thoroughly, and practices in accordance with the Dhamma.

Thus, by resorting to hearing the noble Dhamma, to wise attention, and to practice in accordance with the Dhamma, one understands as it really is: "This is wholesome," and one understands as it really is:

"This is unwholesome. One understands as it really is: "This is blameworthy, this is blameless; this is to be cultivated, this is not to be cultivated; this is inferior, this is superior; this is dark, this is bright, and this is mixed.
For one who knows and sees thus, ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge arises.
With the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, happiness arises, and more than happiness,
gladness arises. Just as, sir, joy might arise in one who is delighted, even so, sir,
with the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, happiness arises, and more than happiness, gladness arises.
“This, sir, is the third attainment of an opportunity discovered by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for the attainment of happiness.
These, sir, are the three attainments of opportunities discovered by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for the attainment of happiness.
This was what Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra said, venerable sir.
"Venerable sir, having spoken on this matter, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:

'What do you think, worthy Tāvatiṃsa devas? How well-proclaimed are these four foundations of mindfulness for the attainment of the wholesome, as they have been proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.'"
Which four?
Here, sir, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
While dwelling contemplating the body in the body internally, he becomes rightly concentrated therein and rightly serene.
Thus, being rightly concentrated and rightly serene therein, he generates knowledge and vision regarding the external bodies of others.
He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings internally...
[and so on] ...he generates knowledge and vision regarding the external feelings of others.
He dwells contemplating the mind within the mind … [and so on] … he generates knowledge and vision regarding the minds of others externally.
He dwells contemplating phenomena within phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“Dwelling contemplating phenomena among internal phenomena, one becomes rightly concentrated therein and rightly serene.
Being rightly concentrated and rightly serene therein, one generates knowledge and vision regarding external phenomena belonging to others.
These, sir, are the four foundations of mindfulness proclaimed by that Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—for the attainment of the wholesome.”
"Venerable sir, this was the meaning spoken by Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra.
Having spoken thus, venerable sir, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
9. The Seven Requisites for Concentration"
“What do you think, worthy devas of the Thirty-three? To what extent have these seven requisites of concentration been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One—
the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One— for the cultivation of right concentration and for the fulfillment of right concentration?”
Which seven?
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.
That one-pointedness of mind which is fully equipped with these seven factors, sir, is called noble right concentration—with its supporting conditions and with its equipment.
For one with right view, friend, right intention arises; for one with right intention, right speech arises; for one with right speech, right action arises.
For one with right action, right livelihood arises; for one with right livelihood, right effort arises;
for one with right effort, right mindfulness arises; for one with right mindfulness, right concentration arises; for one with right concentration...
Right knowledge arises; from right knowledge, right liberation arises.
For if anyone, sir, speaking rightly were to say:

"The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One—it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves; the doors to the Deathless are flung open"—it is precisely this that one would be saying when speaking rightly.

For the Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves, with the doors to the Deathless wide open.

For whoever, sir, is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha, endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma, endowed with verified confidence in the Saṅgha, endowed with the virtues dear to the Noble Ones, and who is one of those born spontaneously—
More than twenty-four hundred thousand Magadhan attendants, disciplined in the Dhamma, have passed away and died;
through the total destruction of the three fetters, they have become stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment.
Among them, there are also once-returners.
The rest of this generation is for their own welfare;
it is my view that they partake of merit,
yet I am not even able to calculate [the extent of it].
“...and fear of speaking falsehood.
This was the meaning, Bhante, that Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra spoke. While Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra was speaking this meaning, Bhante, such a reflection arose in the mind of the Great King Vessavaṇa:

“How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed! Such a sublime Teacher as this will appear; such a sublime proclamation of the Dhamma as this; and such sublime attainments of distinction as these will be known!”
Then, venerable sir, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, having known with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the Great King Vessavaṇa, said this to the Great King Vessavaṇa:
"What does the Great King Vessavaṇa think? In the past, too, there was such a sublime Teacher, such a sublime proclamation of the Dhamma, and such sublime attainments of distinction were manifested."
"In the future too, such a sublime Teacher will appear; such a sublime proclamation of the Dhamma will take place; and such sublime attainments of distinction will be known.
This, venerable sir, was what Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra declared to the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
And this same matter, venerable sir, the Great King Vessavaṇa heard directly from Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra as he was speaking it to the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
“Having received it, he himself announced it to his own assembly.
Thus did the yakkha Janavasabha, having heard this matter directly and received it directly from the Great King Vessavaṇa as he spoke in his own assembly, announce it to the Blessed One.
Having heard this matter directly from the yakkha Janavasabha and received it directly, the Blessed One—

Having learned it himself, he informed the Venerable Ānanda; and the Venerable Ānanda, having heard this matter in the presence of the Blessed One and having received it directly from him, informed the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen.
Thus this holy life has become successful, prosperous, widespread, popular, and extensive, well-proclaimed as far as the world of gods and humans.
The Janavasabha Sutta is finished; it is the fifth.
